propositions.text: The Court must decide how a tree falling in the forest affects taxes if no one replants it.
propositions.quote: the Court is called upon to answer the age-old question: If a tree falls in the forest and you are not around to replant it, how does it affect your taxes?

paragraphs.summary: The Court frames the issue as how a tree falling in the forest affects taxes if no one replants it.

propositions.text: DMI owned forest tenures in Alberta with obligations to reforest after harvesting, which purchasers assumed upon sale.
propositions.quote: DMI was the owner of forest tenures in Alberta under which it was licensed to cut timber...the purchaser of each tenure assumed the obligation to reforest that arose from DMI’s past harvesting.

paragraphs.summary: DMI owned forest tenures in Alberta with reforestation obligations that purchasers assumed upon sale.

propositions.text: The issue is whether DMI must include estimated reforestation costs assumed by purchasers in proceeds of disposition.
propositions.quote: The issue in this case is whether DMI was required to include in its “proceeds of disposition” for each sale an estimate of the cost of the reforestation obligations that the purchasers assumed.

propositions.text: DMI was not required to include reforestation obligations in proceeds of disposition because they depress tenure value and are not separate debts.
propositions.quote: In my view, DMI was not required to do so...The obligation serves to depress the value of the forest tenure. It is not a separate existing debt of the vendor that is assumed by the purchaser as part of the sale price of the forest tenure.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states the issue and concludes DMI need not include reforestation costs in proceeds as they depress tenure value and are not separate debts.

propositions.text: Before 1999, DMI operated two timber divisions with forest tenures allowing timber harvesting under Alberta law.
propositions.quote: DMI operated two timber divisions...each division held a forest tenure that allowed it to cut and remove timber from an area of land owned by the province of Alberta.

propositions.text: The High Level Division’s tenure arose from a Forest Management Agreement; Brewster Lumber’s tenure from timber quotas.
propositions.quote: The High Level Division’s forest tenure arose from a Forest Management Agreement...The Brewster Lumber Division’s forest tenure arose from timber quotas issued by the province.

paragraphs.summary: DMI operated two timber divisions with forest tenures under Alberta law: one from a Forest Management Agreement, the other from timber quotas.

propositions.text: Each tenure required reforestation activities after harvesting, including various silviculture tasks and surveys until 'free-to-grow' status.
propositions.quote: The Forest Management Agreement and timber quotas obliged each division to undertake certain reforestation or silviculture activities...The tenure holder is relieved of its obligation to reforest when it satisfies the province that the reforested area has reached a threshold level of growth, referred to as “free-to-grow” status.

propositions.text: Reforestation generally takes 8-14 years or may be excused if natural events prevent regeneration.
propositions.quote: This process generally takes eight to fourteen years. Alternatively, the province may relieve the holder of its obligation to reforest if natural processes...make it impossible to achieve the regeneration standard.

paragraphs.summary: Each tenure required reforestation activities until 'free-to-grow' status, generally taking 8-14 years or excused by natural events.

propositions.text: In 1999-2000, DMI sold its two timber divisions and their forest tenures, with the High Level Division valued at $169 million plus working capital.
propositions.quote: In 1999 and 2000, DMI sold its High Level and Brewster Lumber divisions...Tolko would pay a purchase price of $169 million...$20 million of the purchase price was allocated to the value of the High Level Division’s forest tenure.

paragraphs.summary: DMI sold its two timber divisions and forest tenures in 1999-2000, with the High Level Division valued at $169 million plus working capital.

propositions.text: The High Level sale agreement required Tolko to assume reforestation obligations estimated at $11 million, with price adjustments after closing.
propositions.quote: The agreement stated that “DMI estimates in good faith that the aggregate value of the current and long term reforestation liabilities will be $11 million”...provided for the purchase price to be adjusted...

paragraphs.summary: The High Level sale required Tolko to assume reforestation obligations estimated at $11 million, with post-closing price adjustments.

propositions.text: Tolko paid $169 million plus working capital; DMI returned $296,225 after final reforestation cost estimate was higher than initial.
propositions.quote: Tolko paid DMI $169 million, plus an additional $16.6 million...DMI tendered a final estimate...$296,225 greater than its initial $11 million estimate. DMI accordingly returned $296,225 to Tolko.

paragraphs.summary: Tolko paid $169 million plus working capital; DMI returned $296,225 after final reforestation cost estimate exceeded initial estimate.

propositions.text: DMI sold Brewster Lumber Division to Seehta for $6.1 million plus working capital; Seehta assumed reforestation obligations without specified cost.
propositions.quote: DMI sold the Brewster Lumber Division...purchase price was $6.1 million...Seehta would assume all obligations to reforest...agreement did not specify an estimated cost.

paragraphs.summary: DMI sold Brewster Lumber Division to Seehta for $6.1 million plus working capital; Seehta assumed reforestation obligations without specified cost.

propositions.text: Alberta consented to tenure assignments only if purchasers undertake reforestation obligations; vendors are relieved of liability upon assignment.
propositions.quote: Alberta approves the assignment of a forest tenure only if the reforestation obligations...are undertaken by the purchaser...the vendor is relieved of any liability...the purchaser is solely responsible.

propositions.text: Alberta says vendor is relieved of liability and purchaser solely responsible for reforestation after assignment.
propositions.quote: Alberta...takes the position that, upon assignment of a forest tenure, the vendor is relieved of any liability...the purchaser is solely responsible for carrying out the reforestation activities.

paragraphs.summary: Alberta consented to tenure assignments only if purchasers undertake reforestation; Alberta says vendors are relieved of liability after assignment.

propositions.text: DMI charged estimated future reforestation costs to earnings but added them back for tax, claiming no tax deduction for those costs.
propositions.quote: DMI charged to earnings the estimated cost of future reforestation obligations...for tax purposes, DMI added back to its income the amounts it had charged to earnings...claimed no tax deduction.

paragraphs.summary: DMI charged estimated future reforestation costs to earnings but added them back for tax, claiming no tax deduction.

propositions.text: DMI increased accounting income on sales to reflect no future reforestation costs but did not include reforestation obligations in tax income.
propositions.quote: DMI increased its income for accounting purposes...In filing its income tax return...DMI did not include in its income any amount to reflect the purchasers’ assumption of the reforestation obligations.

paragraphs.summary: DMI increased accounting income on sales to reflect no future reforestation costs but excluded reforestation obligations from tax income.

propositions.text: Minister reassessed DMI to include estimated reforestation costs assumed by purchasers in proceeds of disposition under Income Tax Act.
propositions.quote: Minister...reassessed DMI...DMI was required to include an amount equal to the estimated cost of the reforestation obligations assumed...in its “proceeds of disposition” under s. 13(21) of the Income Tax Act.

propositions.text: Minister included $11 million for Tolko sale and $2,996,380 for Seehta sale in reassessment; DMI appealed.
propositions.quote: The reassessment included...$11 million for the sale to Tolko...and $2,996,380 for the sale to Seehta...DMI appealed that reassessment.

paragraphs.summary: Minister reassessed DMI to include estimated reforestation costs in proceeds; included $11 million for Tolko and $2,996,380 for Seehta; DMI appealed.

propositions.text: Minister's reassessment did not account for $296,225 returned to Tolko but now says it should have been included.
propositions.quote: The Minister’s reassessment did not account for the $296,225 that DMI returned to Tolko...but has since taken the position that that amount should have been included.

propositions.text: Parties and courts treated $11 million as amount in issue for Tolko sale; Court follows that approach.
propositions.quote: the parties and the courts below have treated that as the amount in issue for the Tolko sale. I do the same in these reasons.

paragraphs.summary: Minister's reassessment omitted $296,225 returned to Tolko but now includes it; parties and courts treat $11 million as issue amount; Court agrees.

propositions.text: Tax Court allowed DMI's appeal in part, holding purchaser's assumption of reforestation obligations must be included in proceeds of disposition.
propositions.quote: Miller J. allowed DMI’s appeal of the Minister’s reassessment in part. He held that...the purchaser’s assumption of reforestation obligations is properly included in the vendor’s proceeds of disposition under s. 13(21) of the Act.

propositions.text: Assumption of reforestation obligations was part of consideration received, based on DMI's admission about price impact.
propositions.quote: it was evident that the assumption of the reforestation obligations was part of the consideration received based on DMI’s admission that...the amount of cash or other consideration it would have paid the Appellant would have increased

paragraphs.summary: Tax Court partly allowed DMI's appeal, finding purchaser's assumption of reforestation obligations was part of consideration received.

propositions.text: Tax Court held it was inappropriate to add full estimated reforestation cost; only near-term costs plus 20% of later costs included.
propositions.quote: Miller J. concluded that DMI should have included...the estimated cost of the reforestation activities that would take place within the 12 months following each sale, plus 20 percent of the estimated cost of the activities that would take place thereafter.

paragraphs.summary: Tax Court found only near-term reforestation costs plus 20% of later costs should be included in proceeds.

propositions.text: Federal Court of Appeal majority held DMI must include entire estimated reforestation costs in proceeds of disposition.
propositions.quote: Nadon J.A. held that DMI was required to include in its proceeds of disposition the entire estimated cost of the reforestation obligations associated with each tenure.

paragraphs.summary: Federal Court of Appeal majority held DMI must include entire estimated reforestation costs in proceeds.

propositions.text: FCA agreed purchaser's assumption of reforestation obligations is consideration received by vendor.
propositions.quote: Nadon J.A. agreed with the Tax Court that a purchaser’s assumption of reforestation obligations amounts to consideration received by the vendor.

propositions.text: FCA majority found Tax Court erred by discounting $11 million estimate; sale agreement value controls.
propositions.quote: the Tax Court erred by treating the $11 million cost...as an estimate that could be discounted for tax purposes...the sale agreement demonstrated...valued the reforestation obligations at $11 million.

paragraphs.summary: FCA majority agreed purchaser's assumption is consideration and Tax Court erred by discounting $11 million estimate; sale agreement value controls.

propositions.text: FCA found Tax Court's reasons inadequate for Brewster sale; remitted for redetermination of reforestation obligation value.
propositions.quote: Nadon J.A. found that the trial judge’s reasons were inadequate...did not address whether...DMI and Seehta had agreed to a value...remitted the matter to the Tax Court for redetermination.

paragraphs.summary: FCA found Tax Court's reasons inadequate for Brewster sale and remitted for redetermination of reforestation obligation value.

propositions.text: Dissenting FCA judge held reforestation obligations are integral to tenure value, not separate consideration to add to proceeds.
propositions.quote: the reforestation obligations “form an integral part of the forest tenures...not a separate consideration...and should thus not be added to the vendor’s proceeds of disposition”

propositions.text: Dissent concluded reforestation liabilities depress property value, so vendor received lower price accordingly.
propositions.quote: The proper approach...is to recognize that the reforestation liabilities...depress the value of the timber resources properties...the vendor...received a lower price...

paragraphs.summary: Dissenting FCA judge held reforestation obligations integral to tenure value, depressing price, not separate consideration to add.

propositions.text: Mainville J.A. would have allowed DMI’s appeal and dismissed the government’s cross-appeal
propositions.quote: Mainville J.A. would have allowed DMI’s appeal and dismissed the government’s cross-appeal.

paragraphs.summary: Mainville J.A. would have allowed DMI’s appeal and dismissed the government’s cross-appeal, as reported by the earlier decision-maker.

propositions.text: Two issues granted for leave: inclusion of reforestation liabilities in proceeds and effect of agreed specific amount
propositions.quote: This Court granted leave on two issues: 1. Are the reforestation liabilities to be included in the proceeds of disposition because the vendor is relieved of a liability or are they integral to and run with the forest tenures? 2. Does it make any difference that the parties agreed to a specific amount of the future reforestation liability?

paragraphs.summary: The Court granted leave on two issues about reforestation liabilities and agreed specific amounts in proceeds of disposition.

propositions.text: Parties agree each forest tenure sold is a timber resource property under Income Tax Act s. 13(21)
propositions.quote: The parties agree that each of the forest tenures sold in this case is a “timber resource property” within the meaning of s. 13(21) of the Income Tax Act because each provides “a right or licence to cut or remove timber from a limit or area in Canada”.

paragraphs.summary: The parties agree each forest tenure sold is a timber resource property under Income Tax Act s. 13(21).

propositions.text: Timber resource property is hybrid: capital property for capital cost allowance but excluded from capital gains treatment
propositions.quote: A timber resource property is treated as a hybrid for tax purposes. On the one hand, it is treated as a capital property for the purposes of capital cost allowance... On the other hand, a timber resource property is excluded from capital gains treatment...

propositions.text: Upon sale, proceeds in excess of capital cost treated as income under Income Tax Act ss. 13(1) and (21)
propositions.quote: Therefore, upon sale of a timber resource property, any proceeds of disposition in excess of the property’s capital cost are treated as income; see Income Tax Act, s. 13(1) and (21)

paragraphs.summary: The court explains timber resource property is hybrid for tax: capital cost allowance applies but gains treated as income under Income Tax Act.

propositions.text: Issue is whether future reforestation costs assumed by purchaser are included in proceeds of disposition
propositions.quote: As set forth above, the issue in this appeal is whether the owner of a forest tenure who sells the tenure must include the estimated amount of future reforestation costs assumed by the purchaser in its proceeds of disposition.

propositions.text: Section 13(21) defines proceeds of disposition to include sale price of property sold
propositions.quote: Section 13(21) of the Income Tax Act defines “proceeds of disposition” to include “the sale price of property that has been sold”.

propositions.text: Focus is whether purchaser’s assumption of reforestation obligations is included in sale price of forest tenure
propositions.quote: The focus of this case is thus on whether the purchasers’ assumption of the reforestation obligations arising from DMI’s previous harvesting is included in the sale price of the forest tenure.

paragraphs.summary: The issue is whether purchaser’s assumption of future reforestation costs is included in proceeds of disposition as part of sale price.

propositions.text: Assumption of vendor’s liability by purchaser may be part of sale price and vendor’s proceeds of disposition
propositions.quote: It is beyond dispute that, as a matter of principle, the assumption of a vendor’s liability by a purchaser may constitute part of the sale price and therefore part of the vendor’s proceeds of disposition; see, e.g., Telus Communications...

propositions.text: Example: purchase of property encumbered by mortgage includes cash plus mortgage assumed in sale price
propositions.quote: A straightforward example of such a circumstance would be the purchase of a property that is encumbered by a mortgage... the sale price of the property includes the amount of the cash received and the amount remaining on the mortgage assumed; see Loyens...

propositions.text: Vendor’s proceeds of disposition include cash and mortgage assumed amounts
propositions.quote: The vendor’s proceeds of disposition for tax purposes would thus include both amounts; see Lord Elgin Hotel Ltd. v. Minister of National Revenue...

paragraphs.summary: The court explains that assumption of vendor’s liability by purchaser may be part of sale price, illustrated by mortgage assumption example.

propositions.text: Minister argues forest tenure with reforestation obligations is like property encumbered by mortgage, so purchaser’s assumption forms part of sale price
propositions.quote: The Minister submits that a forest tenure with reforestation obligations that have arisen under Alberta law from past harvesting is analogous to property encumbered by a mortgage... the purchaser’s assumption of reforestation obligations... must be included in the vendor’s proceeds of disposition.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister argues purchaser’s assumption of reforestation obligations is like mortgage assumption and must be included in proceeds.

propositions.text: DMI and interveners argue analogy to mortgage is misplaced; better analogy is property needing repair which depresses value
propositions.quote: DMI, supported by the industry interveners, submits that the analogy to a mortgage is misplaced... better analogized to property that is in need of repair... need for repairs depresses property’s value.

propositions.text: Purchaser’s assumption of repair costs does not form additional part of sale price even if parties assign value or law requires repairs
propositions.quote: If property in need of repair is sold, the purchaser’s assumption of the cost of repairs does not form an additional part of the sale price... even if the parties attributed a value... and even if the repairs were required by law...

paragraphs.summary: DMI and interveners argue reforestation obligations are like repair costs that depress value, not additional sale price.

propositions.text: Court agrees with DMI and interveners that reforestation obligations are future costs embedded in tenure, not distinct debts forming part of sale price
propositions.quote: I agree with Mainville J.A., DMI and the industry interveners that the assumed reforestation obligations are not appropriately characterized as the assumption of an existing debt of the vendor that forms part of the sale price of the property.

propositions.text: Reforestation obligations are like needed repairs, future costs depressing tenure’s value, unlike mortgage which does not affect property value
propositions.quote: The obligations — much like needed repairs to property — are a future cost embedded in the forest tenure that serves to depress the tenure’s value at the time of sale. This is different from a mortgage...

paragraphs.summary: The court finds reforestation obligations are embedded future costs depressing tenure value, not debts like mortgages.

propositions.text: Alberta law requires consent for forest tenure transfer and purchaser must assume reforestation liability
propositions.quote: Alberta law provides that a forest tenure may be transferred only with the consent of the appropriate provincial official... the Province of Alberta will not approve of a transfer... unless a purchaser assumes the reforestation liability.

propositions.text: Trial judge found and Alberta affirmed that no assumption means no transfer of forest tenures
propositions.quote: the Province effectively forces the purchaser to assume the reforestation liability: no assumption — no transfer of forest tenures”: trial reasons, at para. 26.

propositions.text: Alberta says vendor is absolved of reforestation liability after assignment approval
propositions.quote: Alberta takes the position that, after an assignment has been approved by the province, the vendor is absolved of all liability for the reforestation obligations.

paragraphs.summary: Alberta law requires purchaser to assume reforestation liability for tenure transfer; vendor is absolved after assignment approval.

propositions.text: Alberta’s scheme embeds reforestation obligations in tenure, making them inseparable future costs depressing tenure value
propositions.quote: The effect of Alberta’s scheme is to embed the reforestation obligations into the forest tenure, such that the obligations cannot be severed from the property itself... would decrease the amount such a prospective purchaser would be willing to pay;

propositions.text: Record shows Tolko valued tenure at $31 million less $11 million reforestation cost, tenure value $20 million
propositions.quote: Here, for instance, the record establishes that Tolko valued the High Level Division’s forest tenure at $31 million less the $11 million estimated cost of future reforestation obligations. The forest tenure thus had a value of $20 million.

propositions.text: Including full $31 million in proceeds ignores that DMI did not have $31 million value to sell
propositions.quote: To include the full $31 million in DMI’s proceeds of disposition would disregard the fact that DMI did not have $31 million of value to sell.

paragraphs.summary: Alberta’s scheme embeds reforestation obligations in tenure, reducing its value; full $31 million cannot be proceeds as DMI lacked that value.

propositions.text: Mortgage does not affect property value; property worth $31 million with $11 million mortgage still valued at $31 million
propositions.quote: This distinguishes the reforestation obligations tied to a forest tenure from a mortgage, which does not affect the value of the property it encumbers.

propositions.text: Vendor can obtain $31 million and pay mortgage or $20 million with purchaser assuming mortgage; proceeds equal $31 million
propositions.quote: The vendor of such a property could obtain $31 million for it and then pay off the mortgage. Alternatively, the vendor could obtain $20 million and have the purchaser assume the mortgage... proceeds of disposition to equal the full $31 million because that is the value of the asset being sold.

paragraphs.summary: Mortgage does not reduce property value; vendor’s proceeds equal full property value regardless of mortgage assumption.

propositions.text: Favourable mortgage terms may increase sale price but do not affect property value
propositions.quote: If, for instance, property is encumbered by a mortgage with a very favourable interest rate, it will be more attractive to purchasers who can assume such a mortgage and such purchasers will be prepared to pay more on that account.

propositions.text: Minister analogizes reforestation costs to vendor’s indebtedness on mortgage, but indebtedness does not affect property value
propositions.quote: Here, the Minister analogizes future reforestation costs to the vendor’s indebtedness on a mortgage. As I have explained, the vendor’s indebtedness does not affect the value of the property.

paragraphs.summary: Favourable mortgage terms may affect sale price but not property value; Minister’s analogy to mortgage indebtedness is flawed.

propositions.text: Minister argues reforestation obligations crystallized at sale because obligations incurred and cannot be walked away from
propositions.quote: At the oral hearing, the Minister’s argument was that a forest tenure with reforestation obligations... had “crystallized” by the time of the sale... it had already incurred obligations... and it could not simply walk away from those obligations.

propositions.text: Minister submits DMI benefitted from purchaser’s assumption by amount equal to estimated reforestation cost
propositions.quote: The Minister submits that in these circumstances, DMI benefitted from the purchasers’ assumption of the reforestation obligations by an amount equal to the estimated cost of the reforestation obligations.

paragraphs.summary: Minister argues reforestation obligations crystallized and DMI benefitted from purchaser’s assumption equal to estimated cost.

propositions.text: Meghji for CAPP argues Minister’s argument presupposes reforestation obligations are distinct existing liability
propositions.quote: As Mr. Meghji, arguing for the Canadian Association of Petroleum Producers (“CAPP”), explained... the problem with the Minister’s argument is that it presupposes that the reforestation obligations are a distinct existing liability.

propositions.text: Reforestation obligations are not distinct existing debt but embedded future cost associated with tenure ownership
propositions.quote: As I have explained above, the reforestation obligations were not a distinct existing debt, like a mortgage, but were embedded in the tenure so as to be a future cost associated with ownership of the tenure.

paragraphs.summary: CAPP argues Minister wrongly presumes reforestation obligations are distinct debts; court finds they are embedded future costs.

propositions.text: Alberta’s scheme embeds reforestation obligations in tenure, preventing sale without assigning obligations
propositions.quote: I have concluded that Alberta’s regulatory scheme... has the effect of embedding those reforestation obligations in the tenure itself.

propositions.text: CAPP submits future obligations may be embedded in property rights absent legal requirement preventing sale without assignment
propositions.quote: CAPP submits... statutory obligations to reclaim mined land may be so physically connected to the process of mining itself that the obligations cannot be separated from the property right.

propositions.text: Court need not decide if obligations can be embedded without legal restriction but will not foreclose possibility
propositions.quote: While I need not decide that question on the record before me, I would certainly not foreclose the possibility that obligations associated with a property right could be embedded...

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Alberta’s scheme embeds obligations; CAPP argues obligations may embed without legal restriction; court does not decide.

propositions.text: Reforestation obligations embedded in tenures are future expenses tied to ownership, not separable liabilities forming sale price
propositions.quote: In sum, the reforestation obligations imposed by Alberta law on DMI’s forest tenures are embedded in those tenures and, as such, are future expenses tied to ownership of the property.

propositions.text: Reject Minister’s argument that purchaser’s assumption of reforestation obligations must be added to DMI’s proceeds of disposition
propositions.quote: I would therefore reject the Minister’s argument that the purchasers’ assumption of the reforestation obligations had to be added to DMI’s proceeds of disposition for income tax purposes.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes reforestation obligations are embedded future expenses and rejects Minister’s argument to add them to proceeds.

propositions.text: DMI argues reforestation obligations should not be included as proceeds because they are contingent liabilities
propositions.quote: DMI has also argued that it should not have been required to add the reforestation obligations to its proceeds of disposition because the obligations were a contingent liability.

paragraphs.summary: DMI argues reforestation obligations are contingent liabilities and should not be included in proceeds.

propositions.text: Contingent liability depends on event that may or may not happen; contingent nature affects tax treatment
propositions.quote: A contingent liability is “a liability which depends for its existence upon an event which may or may not happen”: Canada v. McLarty...

propositions.text: No expense incurred for tax if liability is contingent; contingent liabilities not included in capital cost
propositions.quote: In McLarty... no expense is incurred for tax purposes if the liability is contingent... Mandel v. The Queen... a taxpayer may not include in his capital cost a liability to the vendor if the liability is contingent.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains contingent liabilities depend on uncertain events and may not be included for tax expense or capital cost.

propositions.text: DMI’s contingent liability argument is misplaced; it assumes reforestation cost is vendor’s liability not embedded in tenure
propositions.quote: DMI’s argument... is problematic because... it implicitly accepts that the cost of reforestation is a liability of the vendor that is not embedded in the forest tenure...

propositions.text: Reforestation cost is not distinct vendor liability; purchaser’s assumption excluded from proceeds regardless of contingency
propositions.quote: The assumption of the cost of reforestation would thus be excluded from proceeds of disposition independent of whether the cost is absolute or contingent.

propositions.text: Certainty or likelihood of repair cost affects sale price but not whether cost is part of proceeds
propositions.quote: The certainty or likelihood of the cost of repairs may, of course, affect the sale price... It does not, however, affect whether the cost of repairs is part of the proceeds of disposition.

propositions.text: Same applies to reforestation obligations embedded in forest tenure
propositions.quote: The same is true of the reforestation obligations embedded in a forest tenure.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds DMI’s contingent liability argument flawed; reforestation costs embedded in tenure exclude purchaser’s assumption from proceeds regardless of contingency.

propositions.text: Minister's approach causes asymmetry between vendor's proceeds and purchaser's adjusted cost base for forest tenure acquisition.
propositions.quote: The approach advanced by the Minister would lead to asymmetry between the vendor’s proceeds of disposition and the purchaser’s adjusted cost base at the time a forest tenure is acquired.

propositions.text: Minister says purchaser's adjusted cost base excludes estimated reforestation obligations assumed.
propositions.quote: The Minister’s position is that the purchaser’s adjusted cost base upon acquiring a forest tenure does not include the estimated reforestation obligations assumed.

propositions.text: Minister says vendor's proceeds include amount paid plus estimated future reforestation obligations assumed by purchaser.
propositions.quote: the Minister would have the vendor’s proceeds of disposition include the amount paid to the vendor plus an additional amount for the estimated future reforestation obligations assumed by the purchaser.

propositions.text: Adjusted cost base generally includes purchase price plus acquisition expenses or fees.
propositions.quote: a taxpayer’s adjusted cost base generally includes the purchase price of the property, as well as any expenses or fees associated with the acquisition of the property.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Minister's approach causes asymmetry by taxing vendor on reforestation obligations but not including them in purchaser's cost base.

propositions.text: Minister's counsel acknowledged asymmetry at oral hearing.
propositions.quote: Counsel for the Minister acknowledged this asymmetry at the oral hearing.

propositions.text: Under Minister's approach, DMI's taxable proceeds from Tolko sale would be $31 million, but Tolko's adjusted cost base would be $20 million.
propositions.quote: Under the Minister’s approach, the sale of the High Level Division to Tolko would have resulted in taxable proceeds of $31 million for DMI ($20 million received plus $11 million in assumed reforestation obligations). However, Tolko’s adjusted cost base would be $20 million (just the amount paid).

propositions.text: Minister's approach means Tolko would be taxed on $11 million income without receiving it if it sold immediately.
propositions.quote: Tolko would be assessed $11 million of taxable income, despite in no way receiving such additional income.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Minister's counsel admitted asymmetry causing Tolko to be taxed on income it did not receive.

propositions.text: Purchaser's assumption of reforestation obligations does not form part of vendor's proceeds of disposition, avoiding asymmetry.
propositions.quote: The conclusion I have reached — that a purchaser’s assumption of reforestation obligations does not form part of the vendor’s proceeds of disposition — avoids this asymmetry.

propositions.text: Mainville J.A. recognized that an interpretation promoting symmetry and fairness is preferred.
propositions.quote: as Mainville J.A. recognized in his dissent, an interpretation of the Act that promotes symmetry and fairness through a harmonious taxation scheme is to be preferred over an interpretation which promotes neither value.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes excluding reforestation obligations from vendor's proceeds avoids asymmetry, citing Mainville J.A.'s preference for fairness.

propositions.text: Minister reassessed DMI using $11 million estimate for Tolko sale and DMI's internal estimates for Seehta sale.
propositions.quote: The Minister reassessed DMI with respect to the Tolko sale using the $11 million estimated cost of the reforestation obligations included in the sale agreement and reassessed DMI with respect to the Seehta sale using DMI’s internal accounting estimates.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal majority held inclusion of reforestation costs depends on agreement to estimated future cost.
propositions.quote: According to the majority of the Court of Appeal, whether reforestation costs should be included in proceeds of disposition turns on whether the contracting parties agreed to an estimated future cost.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal upheld Minister's reassessment for Tolko sale but remitted Seehta sale for trial judge to determine agreement on cost.
propositions.quote: It thus upheld the Minister’s reassessment in the Tolko sale, but remitted the matter to the trial judge to determine whether there was an agreement as to the cost in the Seehta sale.

paragraphs.summary: The court reports Minister's reassessments and Court of Appeal's majority ruling on agreement to estimated costs affecting inclusion in proceeds.

propositions.text: DMI's proceeds do not depend on parties agreeing to specific estimate of reforestation costs in sale agreement.
propositions.quote: DMI’s proceeds of disposition do not depend on whether the contracting parties agreed to a specific estimate of the cost of those obligations in their sale agreement.

propositions.text: Amount assigned to reforestation obligations is a factor in determining fair market value of forest tenures.
propositions.quote: Any amount that the parties assigned to the reforestation obligations in the sale agreement was simply a factor in determining the fair market value of the forest tenures

paragraphs.summary: The court holds proceeds do not depend on agreed estimate; assigned amounts only affect fair market value determination.

propositions.text: DMI's accounting estimates for reforestation costs are irrelevant for tax purposes under the Income Tax Act.
propositions.quote: It is also irrelevant that DMI estimated the cost of future reforestation to compute its income for accounting purposes.

propositions.text: Income Tax Act does not permit accounting approach of deducting and adding back reforestation obligations.
propositions.quote: the Income Tax Act does not permit that approach

propositions.text: Financial accounting and income tax calculation have distinct purposes, per Canderel Ltd. v. Canada.
propositions.quote: This Court has recognized the distinct purposes of financial accounting and income tax calculation: Canderel Ltd. v. Canada, [1998] 1 S.C.R. 147, at para. 36.

propositions.text: Including DMI's accounting estimates in proceeds of disposition would be an error.
propositions.quote: It would thus be an error to simply include DMI’s accounting estimates in its proceeds of disposition.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds DMI's accounting estimates irrelevant for tax and including them in proceeds would be erroneous.

propositions.text: DMI was not required to include future reforestation costs assumed by Tolko and Seehta in taxable proceeds.
propositions.quote: DMI was not required to include in its taxable proceeds of disposition an amount reflecting the future reforestation costs assumed by Tolko and Seehta.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes DMI need not include future reforestation costs in taxable proceeds.

propositions.text: Appeal is allowed with costs to DMI and matter remitted to Minister for reassessment per these reasons.
propositions.quote: The appeal is allowed with costs throughout to DMI and the matter is remitted to the Minister for reassessment in accordance with these reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the appeal with costs and remits the matter to the Minister for reassessment.
